titre: The Kuleshov effect is taught everywhere; the film that founded it remains missing
accroche: Every film school cites Kuleshov's editing experiment. No filmed trace of it has ever been found.
contenu_vulgarise:
The textbook always describes the same scene: three identical shots of the impassive face of the actor Ivan Mozzhukhin, each cut together with a different image, a bowl of soup, a woman in a coffin, a little girl playing. The audience praises the subtlety of the actor's performance, which seems to express in turn hunger, grief, then desire. The face, however, is strictly the same frame copied three times: it is the editing alone, the mere juxtaposition of shots, that manufactures the emotion attributed to the actor.

## An edit that no one has ever seen again

The anecdote comes from a workshop opened in Moscow in 1919-1920 by the filmmaker Lev Kuleshov, within the brand-new State School of Cinematography. In the middle of the civil war, film stock is so scarce that Kuleshov has his students, including the future filmmaker Vsevolod Pudovkin, work without shooting anything themselves: they re-edit existing foreign films, including D. W. Griffith's *Intolerance*, changing the order and assembly of shots to observe what that change alone does to meaning. The idea that cinema builds its meaning through editing, more than through the content of each shot taken in isolation, becomes the theoretical foundation of Soviet cinema, taken up and amplified a few years later by Sergei Eisenstein. It is from this workshop that the Mozzhukhin face experiment is born, between 1918 and 1921. But no reel, no set photograph, no document of the period attests to this particular edit. The only accounts of it come from Kuleshov himself and from Pudovkin, years later, in texts that disagree on the details: which images exactly, how many shots, in what order.

## What this shifts

Uncertainty about the origin has not kept the Kuleshov effect from becoming one of the pillars of editing as taught, nor psychologists from wanting to measure it ever since. The results, though, diverge. In 1992, a study of 137 participants finds no effect. In 2006, a team using brain imaging does observe an effect, but only with neutral faces. In 2016, the most careful replication of the protocol, published in the journal Perception, confirms the 2006 result, and notes in the same article that no filmed or photographic trace of the original experiment is known, and that the historical accounts describing it contradict one another. The paradox closes in on itself: the psychological phenomenon Kuleshov named seems real, under certain precise conditions, while the founding story that has illustrated it for a century in every film textbook has never been verified.

repere.texte: The reference study on the question, published in 2016 in the journal Perception, states it plainly: no filmed or photographic trace of Kuleshov's original experiment is known, if such an edit was ever actually put together, and the few accounts of it, by Kuleshov and Pudovkin themselves, contradict each other on the details as early as the 1920s.
repere.source: Barratt, Cabak Rédei, Innes-Ker, van de Weijer, Does the Kuleshov Effect Really Exist?, Perception, vol. 45, no. 8, 2016

carte.punch: Kuleshov's experiment, taught in every textbook, left no filmed trace.
carte.idee: Film textbooks describe the Kuleshov effect: the same face, cut with three images, seems to express three emotions. But no filmed or photographic trace of the experiment, carried out in Moscow around 1920, is known: only contradictory accounts by Kuleshov and Pudovkin speak of it.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: A full overview of the historical accounts of the experiment and of modern scientific attempts at replication.

quiz.question: What do we actually know about the edit that supposedly produced the Kuleshov effect on the face of the actor Ivan Mozzhukhin?
choix: The original edit was found in 1956 in the archives of Soviet cinema
It only ever existed as a plan, never carried out for lack of film stock
The edit was deliberately destroyed by Soviet censorship in 1934
No filmed trace exists; only later accounts by Kuleshov and Pudovkin speak of it
quiz.explication: Nothing indicates a rediscovery in 1956, a destruction by censorship in 1934, or a plan left without follow-up: Kuleshov's workshop did indeed re-edit existing films for lack of new film stock. What is missing is a material trace of this particular edit; only later, discordant accounts by Kuleshov and Pudovkin speak of it, years after the fact.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where and when does Lev Kuleshov open the workshop from which the experiment on Mozzhukhin's face is born?
choix: In Moscow, in 1919-1920, within the State School of Cinematography
In Saint Petersburg, in 1925, in a private studio
In Moscow, in 1934, under the control of Soviet censorship
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text places Kuleshov's workshop in Moscow, opened in 1919-1920 within the State School of Cinematography, in the middle of the civil war and a film-stock shortage.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which film do Kuleshov and his students re-edit, unable to shoot anything themselves?
choix: The Birth of a Nation, by D. W. Griffith
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that the workshop re-edits D. W. Griffith's Intolerance, changing the order and assembly of shots to observe the effect of editing on meaning.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the study published in 2016 in the journal Perception find about the Kuleshov effect?
choix: That it never occurs, whatever face is shown
That it is stronger with faces already expressing a marked emotion
That it confirms the effect observed in 2006, but only on neutral faces
That it was measured for the first time thanks to the original reel being found
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text indicates that the 2016 study, the most careful, confirms the 2006 result: a measurable effect, but only with neutral faces, not with already marked expressions.
